title: Sampling and investigating populations; Ecosystems, populations and niches
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EC01a#t1 term and clue written for the game; EC02#t3 term and clue written for the game; EC01a#t4 term and clue written for the game; EC02#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EC01a#N.3a, EC02#N.4, EC01a#N.5, EC02#N.14, EC01a#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Population
items.clue: All the organisms of one species in one area at one time

items.label: Frequency
items.clue: Proportion of quadrats (as %) in which the species occurs

items.label: Abiotic factors
items.clue: Non-living influences such as temperature, light, pH and salinity

items.label: Belt transect
items.clue: Quadrats placed along a line, continuously or at regular intervals

questions.stem: Two groups of great crested newts breed in ponds 5 km apart, and no newt ever moves between the ponds. How should the two groups be described?

options.text: Two populations of one species, because the groups are reproductively isolated from each other.
Two species, because groups that do not interbreed cannot belong to the same species.
One population, because all the newts belong to the same species, wherever they breed.
Two communities, because each pond contains newts together with the other organisms living in it.

questions.stem: A student places ten 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrats at random in a 250 m² meadow and counts 20 orchids in total. What is the estimated population of orchids in the meadow?

options.text: 2000 plants
20 plants
500 plants
20000 plants

questions.explanation: Each quadrat is 0.25 m², so the sampled area is 10 × 0.25 = 2.5 m². Density = 20 ÷ 2.5 = 8 orchids per m², and 8 × 250 m² = 2000 orchids.

questions.stem: A student finds a woodland plant only on the shaded side of a hedge. Which pair names one abiotic factor and one biotic factor that could explain this?

options.text: Light intensity; soil pH
A grazing rabbit; a competing grass
Light intensity; a competing grass
Soil water; air temperature

questions.explanation: Light is non-living (abiotic); a competitor is living (biotic). Either could restrict the plant to the shaded side.

questions.stem: A student estimates the number of dandelions on a school field. She places ten quadrats in the spots where she can see dandelions growing, counts carefully, and scales up by the area of the field. Which statement about her estimate is correct?

options.text: It will be accurate, because she counted every dandelion in each quadrat carefully.
It will be exact if she places fifty quadrats the same way instead of ten.
It is likely to be too high, because the quadrats were not placed at random.
Choosing spots with dandelions is better than random placement, because it gives typical samples.

questions.explanation: She sampled only where dandelions grow, so her mean density is higher than the field's. Random coordinates give every point an equal chance.

questions.stem: A fallen, rotting log in a wood holds beetle larvae, woodlice, fungi and bacteria. Inside it are damp, decaying wood and still air. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The log cannot be an ecosystem, because an ecosystem must cover a large area such as a forest.
The log's organisms, with its damp wood and still air, form a small ecosystem.
All the organisms living in the log together form one population.
The fungi and bacteria are not part of the community, because they are neither animals nor plants.

questions.explanation: A community plus its abiotic environment is an ecosystem, whether it is a log, a rock pool or a rainforest.
